parts.say:
So the offer of the Dutch West India Company was received and in due course of time the provisions were put into writing. The Pilgrim company discussed the offer from every angle. All of them would have preferred to settle under the British flag, if it could have been arranged, but because more than six months had passed and they had not found anyone who could finance them, they felt that the Dutch offer should be accepted.
Therefore, near the end of February, 1620, Pastor Robinson and Elder Carver meet with Wilhelm Kieft to settle finally the matter of the emigration. Let us listen as they talk together.

parts.say: Aye. 'Tis a goodly country--full as rich as Virginia.

lines.text: Aye. 'Tis a goodly country--full as rich as Virginia.

parts.say:
So the _Mayflower_ brought up to anchor just inside Cape Cod, near the present village of Provincetown. The voyage had been long and arduous. There had been much sickness aboard, and Captain Jones knew that most of the passengers longed to set foot on solid ground and begin the task of building their homes. So he determined to create further dissatisfaction among them.
For our next scene we are going into Captain Jones's cabin just as one of the five men of the company, Peter Brown, has come into the cabin on the captain's invitation.

So the _Mayflower_ brought up to anchor just inside Cape Cod, near the present village of Provincetown. The voyage had been long and arduous. There had been much sickness aboard, and Captain Jones knew that most of the passengers longed to set foot on solid ground and begin the task of building their homes. So he determined to create further dissatisfaction among them.
For our next scene we are going into Captain Jones's cabin just as one of the five men of the company, Peter Brown, has come into the cabin on the captain's invitation.

parts.say: Sit you down, Master Brown, and find what comfort you can in my poor quarters.

lines.text: Sit you down, Master Brown, and find what comfort you can in my poor quarters.

parts.say: Poor! If this cabin is poor, Captain, what do ye call what us folks has to put up with, all crowded into the common cabin like sheep er worse?

lines.text: Poor! If this cabin is poor, Captain, what do ye call what us folks has to put up with, all crowded into the common cabin like sheep er worse?

parts.say: Aye, 'tis too bad the cabin is not a better place for your goodly company.

lines.text: Aye, 'tis too bad the cabin is not a better place for your goodly company.

parts.say: Aye, well, we'll soon be out of it.

lines.text: Aye, well, we'll soon be out of it.

parts.say: I fear me, not so soon.

lines.text: I fear me, not so soon.

parts.say: Indeed, why?

lines.text: Indeed, why?

parts.say: The ship must be repaired before we can go on.

lines.text: The ship must be repaired before we can go on.

parts.say: How long will that take ye?

lines.text: How long will that take ye?

parts.say: Mayhap two months or more, I know not.

lines.text: Mayhap two months or more, I know not.

parts.say: Two months? Two months more in the cabin of this ship and half of our company will be dead.

lines.text: Two months? Two months more in the cabin of this ship and half of our company will be dead.

parts.say: Aye, belikes they will--and winter will be upon us hard and heavy. The winters in this country are worse than any you have ever seen in England or Holland.

lines.text: Aye, belikes they will--and winter will be upon us hard and heavy. The winters in this country are worse than any you have ever seen in England or Holland.

parts.say: Indeed!

lines.text: Indeed!

parts.say: The snow lies so deep it would cover a man's head--the land is blotted out, and even the sea freezes--

lines.text: Then how could we get ashore?

parts.say: I know not.

lines.text: I know not.

parts.say: And once ashore, how could we find a fair place to build our homes?

lines.text: And once ashore, how could we find a fair place to build our homes?

parts.say: 'Tis not for me to say.

lines.text: 'Tis not for me to say.

parts.say: Why can't we land right here, Captain?

lines.text: Why can't we land right here, Captain?

parts.say: Because your Elder, Master Carver, says fix the ship and go on.

lines.text: Because your Elder, Master Carver, says fix the ship and go on.

parts.say: If Elder Carver says that, then there be naught that we kin do.

lines.text: If Elder Carver says that, then there be naught that we kin do.

parts.say: You'd stay packed in the ship's cabin, facing sickness and death, rather than rise up like men and tell the Elder what you will and what you won't do, eh?

lines.text: You'd stay packed in the ship's cabin, facing sickness and death, rather than rise up like men and tell the Elder what you will and what you won't do, eh?

parts.say: Elder Carver and the twelve masters have the voice; we have naught to do but to obey.

lines.text: Elder Carver and the twelve masters have the voice; we have naught to do but to obey.

parts.say: Can it be that forty English freemen can't vote down twelve masters?

lines.text: Can it be that forty English freemen can't vote down twelve masters?

parts.say: Under our charter the freemen have no voice.

lines.text: Under our charter the freemen have no voice.

parts.say: Under the charter, eh?

lines.text: Under the charter, eh?

parts.say: Aye, so there's naught to do but what the masters say.

lines.text: Aye, so there's naught to do but what the masters say.

parts.say: Have you never heard of mutiny?

lines.text: Have you never heard of mutiny?

parts.say: Mutiny? Nay, we be lawful men, bound together in the love of Jehovah; we'll not mutiny! We must abide by our charter.

lines.text: Mutiny? Nay, we be lawful men, bound together in the love of Jehovah; we'll not mutiny! We must abide by our charter.

parts.say: The charter, aye.

lines.text: The charter, aye.

parts.say: So there's naught to do--

lines.text: So there's naught to do--

parts.say: Hold--have you thought on this--the charter binds you under the King's grant in Virginia Plantation--

lines.text: Hold--have you thought on this--the charter binds you under the King's grant in Virginia Plantation--

parts.say: Aye.

lines.text: Aye.

parts.say: And you are not in Virginia--

lines.text: And you are not in Virginia--

parts.say: Nay, not yet.

lines.text: Nay, not yet.

parts.say: So you are not bound by the Virginia charter in these waters.

lines.text: So you are not bound by the Virginia charter in these waters.

parts.say: Forsooth, Captain, I'd not thought on that.

lines.text: Forsooth, Captain, I'd not thought on that.

parts.say: You have here all the rights of free-born Englishmen. And if you rise like men and demand that your Elders hearken to your voice, who shall gainsay you?

lines.text: You have here all the rights of free-born Englishmen. And if you rise like men and demand that your Elders hearken to your voice, who shall gainsay you?

parts.say: Aye--who--who, indeed? If we vote to land here, 'tis not mutiny.

lines.text: Aye--who--who, indeed? If we vote to land here, 'tis not mutiny.

parts.say: Nay, 'tis but your right, if you want to land here.

lines.text: Nay, 'tis but your right, if you want to land here.

parts.say: We do--we do! Not a man in the company but would stay here if he had his way.

lines.text: We do--we do! Not a man in the company but would stay here if he had his way.

parts.say: Then have your way--like Englishmen! Go to your cabin. Talk to the men of your company, tell them what I have told you.

lines.text: Then have your way--like Englishmen! Go to your cabin. Talk to the men of your company, tell them what I have told you.

parts.say: Aye, Captain, I will! At once.

lines.text: Aye, Captain, I will! At once.

parts.say: Good!
Well, Elder Carver, we shall see whose voice is stronger--yours, or the voice of forty English freemen!

lines.text: Good!  Well, Elder Carver, we shall see whose voice is stronger--yours, or the voice of forty English freemen!

parts.say: Thus Captain Jones planted in the mind of one of the freemen of the Pilgrim company an idea which he was sure would bear fruit before many hours. He watched the company as first one man and then another fell in with Peter Brown. He felt the temper of the company changing, but he still did not feel that mutiny was likely against the strong religious authority of the Elders. parts.say: I fear me, Master Carver, we are in a bad way.

parts.say: The carpenter has gone over the ship timber by timber--

parts.say: Well?

parts.say: Oh, too bad, too bad! How long?

lines.text: Oh, too bad, too bad! How long?

parts.say: What with finding the proper timbers ashore, and hewing them to fit our needs, I fear it may well be two months or more before we can leave these waters.

lines.text: What with finding the proper timbers ashore, and hewing them to fit our needs, I fear it may well be two months or more before we can leave these waters.

lines.text: Then our stores are in danger of being ruined.

lines.text: Aye, they are even now in such danger they should be unshipped.

lines.text: Then we must do it--set your crew to the work at once.

parts.say: The crew has more than it can do to repair the ship and make it ready to sail on to Virginia, since you insist on going on.

parts.say: Men of the Pilgrim company, as no doubt you are all well aware by now, the land we made this morning with such joy and thanksgiving in our hearts is not the land of the Virginia Plantation.

lines.text: Men of the Pilgrim company, as no doubt you are all well aware by now, the land we made this morning with such joy and thanksgiving in our hearts is not the land of the Virginia Plantation.

parts.say: Aye, we know as much! So we have heard.

lines.text: Aye, we know as much! So we have heard.

parts.say: But our ship is sore distressed from the buffeting of the storms, and Captain Jones must needs make repairs before we can sail on to our destination.
I would it were not so, for I know how weary you find yourselves after the many days upon the sea. But there's naught else to do.

parts.say: Nay, nay, it cannot be. This is not Virginia; we have no patent to these lands. We must sail on. The captain and his crew will make their repairs as soon as they can, but our stores in the hold are all of them in danger of spoiling--so we must needs unship them ourselves until such time as we may sail away from here. So let every man prepare himself for work.

parts.say: It may be for the best interest of the company and for the glory of Jehovah. I consent to your wishes.
But it behooves us to enter into a compact, one with the other--that no man may say, once we have landed in New England, that we have no law and cannot punish the disobedient.

parts.say: May it please ye, sir, we be more than willing for the masters to write a compact that all can sign to be governed like any free-born Englishmen by the will o' the majority--

parts.say: So be it--let the masters of the company join me in my cabin, and we shall make a compact joining all the company of freemen into a body politic.

parts.say: And so in the cabin of the _Mayflower_ the masters of the company, twelve in number, met in the first American legislative assembly and drew up one of the most famous documents in American history--the Mayflower Compact--which organized the first self-governing community in the New World.
